fading-001.question: Where there is no line-of-sight direct wave and only many reflected and scattered waves arrive, the received level fluctuates wildly when the receiver moves slightly. Which distribution is the envelope (amplitude) of the received signal taken to follow in this case?
choices: Log-normal distribution
Rayleigh distribution
Uniform distribution
fading-001.explanation: When many scattered waves add up with random phases, the central limit theorem makes the in-phase and quadrature components of the received signal each follow a zero-mean normal distribution. Their envelope √(I² + Q²) then follows a Rayleigh distribution, and the power follows an exponential distribution. This is Rayleigh fading, in which deep fades appear about every half wavelength of movement. The log-normal distribution is used for shadowing, in which obstruction by buildings and the like changes the average level over ranges of tens of meters or more. Because the waves combine without aligned phases, the amplitude is not uniformly distributed; small amplitudes are less likely, but deep fades still occur a definite fraction of the time.

fading-002.question: Which statement about the K-factor of Rician fading (the ratio of the direct-wave power to the total scattered-wave power) is correct?
choices: When K is 0 it is the same as Rayleigh fading, and the larger K is, the smaller the fluctuation of the received level
The larger K is, the larger the share of scattered-wave power, so the fades become deeper than in Rayleigh fading
When K is 1, the direct and scattered waves have equal power and cancel each other, so the fluctuation of the received level is smallest
fading-002.explanation: Rician fading is the state in which scattered waves add to a strong direct wave (such as a line-of-sight wave), and the envelope follows a Rician distribution. The K-factor is the power ratio of the direct wave to the scattered waves, and with no direct wave, K = 0, it matches the Rayleigh distribution. The larger K is, the more the steady direct wave dominates and the smaller the relative fluctuation from the scattered waves; for very large K the channel approaches one with no fading. The scattered waves are strong when K is small, so the choice saying that a larger K means stronger scattered waves has it backward. K = 1 is an intermediate state in which the direct and scattered waves have equal power, not the state of smallest fluctuation. K becomes large in outdoor links with line of sight and in links where high-gain antennas are pointed at each other.

fading-003.question: Which statement about the fluctuation of the received level when receiving on the move is correct?
choices: Multipath fading occurs only when the line of sight is blocked and the receiver enters the shadow of a building, and it changes slowly over ranges of several km according to the size of the obstruction
Shadowing is caused by interference between waves reflected from buildings; it is a fast, Rayleigh-distributed fluctuation with deep fades about every half wavelength of movement
The received level can be treated as the sum of the average attenuation with distance, shadowing that changes over tens of meters or more, and multipath fading that changes over about a wavelength
fading-003.explanation: The received level in mobile reception is considered as three fluctuations of different scales. First comes the path loss that falls on average with distance, expressed by the path loss exponent. Next is shadowing caused by obstruction from buildings and terrain, which changes slowly over ranges of tens of meters or more depending on the size of the obstacles, and whose dB value is treated as normally distributed (a log-normal distribution). Finally there is fading from multipath interference, a fast fluctuation with deep fades over movements of about half a wavelength. The choice that has multipath fading change slowly over several km and the choice that calls shadowing a fast fluctuation every half wavelength both mix up the scales of these two fluctuations. In link design, separate margins for shadowing and for fading are added to the average loss.

fading-004.question: In Rayleigh fading, the received power p follows an exponential distribution with mean p̄, and the probability that p falls below x·p̄ is 1 − e⁻ˣ. Which is closest to the probability that the received power is 20 dB or more below the mean?
choices: About 10%
About 1%
About 0.01%
fading-004.explanation: 20 dB below means x = 0.01, and the probability is 1 − exp(−0.01) ≈ 0.00995, about 1%. For small x, 1 − e⁻ˣ ≈ x, so each additional 10 dB of fade depth cuts the probability by about 1/10. About 10% is the probability of falling 10 dB below (1 − exp(−0.1) ≈ 0.095), a mistake in converting dB to a ratio. About 0.01% wrongly takes the probability as x²; that corresponds to selection diversity with two independent antennas. In Rayleigh fading, a margin of about 20 dB is needed just to keep reception at 99% of times or places, which is the motivation for using diversity.

fading-005.question: Which is closest to the coherence bandwidth of a channel whose delay spread (rms delay) στ is 1 µs? Take the coherence bandwidth as Bc ≈ 1/(5στ) (the guideline for a frequency correlation of 0.5).
choices: 200 kHz
1 MHz
5 MHz
fading-005.explanation: Bc ≈ 1/(5 × 1×10⁻⁶ s) = 2×10⁵ Hz = 200 kHz. At two frequencies separated by well more than this, fades occur almost independently. 1 MHz drops the factor and uses 1/στ, and 5 MHz applies the factor the wrong way round. The factor depends on the correlation value used in the definition, and forms such as 1/(50στ) (correlation 0.9) are also used, so note that it is only a guideline. Under any definition, the larger the delay spread (the more waves arrive late), the narrower the coherence bandwidth.

fading-006.question: What happens when the signal bandwidth is much wider than the coherence bandwidth of the channel?
choices: Because a wider band averages out the fades at individual frequencies, the result is flat fading, in which all frequencies in the band fade in the same way
The Doppler spread grows in proportion to the bandwidth, giving time-selective fading in which the received level changes quickly even within one symbol
Frequency-selective fading, in which the fades differ with frequency across the band; in the time domain, delayed waves overlap the next symbol, causing intersymbol interference
fading-006.explanation: The coherence bandwidth is the range over which the frequency response of the channel can be regarded as nearly the same. If the signal band is wider than this, the amplitude and phase differ across the band, and notches appear in the spectrum. In the time domain, the delay spread becomes comparable to or longer than the symbol duration, so delayed waves overlap the next symbol and cause intersymbol interference, which needs countermeasures such as an equalizer. Flat fading, in which the whole band fades in the same way, is the opposite case, where the signal band is narrower than the coherence bandwidth. Time selectivity is set by the Doppler spread and is a separate property from the relation between bandwidth and coherence bandwidth. OFDM divides a wide band into narrow subcarriers so that each subcarrier can be treated as flat fading.

fading-007.question: A terminal moving at 72 km/h (20 m/s) receives a 3.5 GHz radio wave. Which is closest to the maximum Doppler frequency? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: About 233 Hz
About 467 Hz
About 840 Hz
fading-007.explanation: The wavelength is λ = c/f ≈ 0.0857 m, and the maximum Doppler frequency is fD = v/λ = 20/0.0857 ≈ 233 Hz. In mobile communication, waves arrive from many directions around the terminal, and each is shifted by fD cos α according to its angle α to the direction of travel, so the received spectrum spreads from −fD to +fD (Doppler spread). About 467 Hz wrongly uses the radar formula 2v/λ, which applies to a round trip; for one-way communication it is v/λ. About 840 Hz is a unit error that substitutes the speed as 72, the value in km/h.

fading-008.question: Which statement about the quantities that characterize a multipath channel is correct?
choices: The larger the delay spread, the faster the phases of the delayed waves rotate, so the received level changes quickly over time even when the terminal and its surroundings are still
The Doppler spread sets how fast the channel changes over time, and the shorter the coherence time, which is inversely proportional to it, the faster the channel changes
The coherence time is set by the delay spread: the larger the delay spread, the shorter the coherence time and the faster the state of the channel changes
fading-008.explanation: A multipath channel is characterized by two spreads, one in frequency and one in time. The delay spread sets the variation across frequency (coherence bandwidth and frequency selectivity), and the Doppler spread sets the variation over time. Over the coherence time, which is inversely proportional to the maximum Doppler frequency fD (Tc ≈ 0.423/fD as a guideline; depending on the correlation used in the definition, forms such as 9/(16πfD) ≈ 0.179/fD are also used), the channel can be regarded as nearly unchanged; for example, with fD = 100 Hz, Tc ≈ 4.2 ms. The choices that tie the speed of change over time, or the coherence time, to the delay spread swap the roles of delay spread and Doppler spread. The two are separate properties: even with a large delay spread, no change over time occurs if the transmitter, receiver and surroundings are all stationary.

fading-009.question: Which statement about the relation between the symbol duration and the coherence time is correct?
choices: The longer the symbol duration is compared with the coherence time, the more the channel variation is averaged out within one symbol, so amplitude and phase are easy to correct even with widely spaced pilots
The coherence time is set by the symbol rate: doubling the symbol rate doubles the coherence time

If the symbol duration is much shorter than the coherence time, the channel is nearly constant during one symbol, but a fade lasts over many symbols, so interleaving spreads the errors to let error correction work
fading-009.explanation: In slow fading, where the symbol duration is shorter than the coherence time, the channel can be regarded as nearly constant during a symbol (or from one pilot to the next), so the amplitude and phase can be corrected with the estimated channel. A fade, however, lasts about as long as the coherence time, so the consecutive symbols during it are all in error together, a burst error. Interleaving, which reorders the transmitted bits, scatters the errors so that the error-correcting code can work. If the symbol duration is longer than the coherence time, the channel changes within one symbol (fast fading) and correction becomes difficult, so the choice saying that a symbol longer than the coherence time sees less channel change has it backward. The coherence time is set by the speed of movement and the frequency, not by the symbol rate.

fading-010.question: Selection diversity, which picks the antenna with the larger received power, is used with two antennas that undergo independent Rayleigh fading (with equal average received power). If the probability that the received power of a single antenna is 20 dB or more below the mean is 1%, which is closest to the probability that both antennas are 20 dB or more below the mean at the same time?
choices: About 2%
About 0.5%
About 0.01%
fading-010.explanation: With selection diversity, reception fails only when both antennas fade at the same time. If the two are independent, the probabilities multiply: 0.01 × 0.01 = 10⁻⁴, about 0.01%. Achieving the same 0.01% with one antenna would need a margin down to 40 dB below the mean, so at the same probability the required margin has dropped by about 20 dB (diversity gain). About 2% wrongly adds the probabilities, and about 0.5% wrongly divides by 2; both miss the point that independent fades rarely happen at the same time. If the antennas are correlated, the improvement is smaller.

fading-011.question: Which statement about maximal ratio combining (MRC) diversity is correct? Assume the noise in each branch is uncorrelated and equal in power.
choices: It aligns the phases of the branch signals and adds them with weights proportional to their amplitudes, and the combined S/N is the sum of the branch S/Ns
It outputs only the branch with the largest S/N at each instant and discards the signals of all the other branches without using them in the combination
It aligns the phases of all branches and adds them with equal weights, and the combined S/N is the product of the branch S/Ns
fading-011.explanation: Maximal ratio combining aligns the phases of the branch signals and adds them with weights proportional to their amplitudes (when the noise is equal). The combined S/N is then the sum of the branch S/Ns, the largest of any linear combining method. Combining four branches with an average S/N of 10 dB each gives four times the average S/N, about 16 dB, and deep fades are reduced at the same time. Selecting only the largest is selection diversity; its circuit is simple, but the improvement is smaller than with maximal ratio combining. Adding with aligned phases and equal weights is equal-gain combining, and with no method does the S/N become a product.

fading-012.question: Which statement about antenna spacing for space diversity is correct?
choices: For both terminals and base stations, regardless of the angular spread, the fading correlation does not drop unless the antennas are at least one wavelength apart, so no diversity effect at all is obtained

A terminal, with waves arriving from many directions around it, needs only about half a wavelength for low correlation, but a tall base station with a small angular spread needs several to more than ten wavelengths
The required antenna spacing depends neither on wavelength nor on angular spread; for both terminals and base stations, at least 10 cm is enough at any frequency
fading-012.explanation: The spacing at which the fading of two antennas becomes nearly uncorrelated depends on how wide a range of angles the waves arrive from. For a terminal, where waves arrive from all directions off surrounding buildings, the correlation first drops to near zero at a spacing of about 0.4λ, so about half a wavelength gives a diversity effect. Seen from a base station mounted high up, however, the scatterers are clustered around the terminal and the angular spread is small, so a spacing of several to more than ten wavelengths is needed. Terminals benefit even with less than one wavelength, so the choice requiring at least one wavelength is wrong, and the required spacing scales with wavelength, so it is not a fixed length either. Polarization diversity can create nearly independent branches without any spacing.

fading-013.question: In the two-ray model, which considers a ground-reflected wave and a direct wave, which is correct about the received power when the distance d between transmitter and receiver is large enough (beyond the breakpoint)? Assume the antenna heights ht and hr and the antenna gains are constant.
choices: Like free space, it is inversely proportional to the square of distance (falling about 6 dB when the distance doubles), gets smaller at higher frequencies, and does not depend on the antenna heights
It falls as the fourth power of distance (about 12 dB when the distance doubles), is approximately independent of frequency, and is proportional to the square of the product of the antenna heights

As the path difference approaches zero, the direct and reflected waves add in phase, so it stays nearly constant regardless of distance and always exceeds the free-space value, whatever the antenna heights
fading-013.explanation: At long range, the path difference 2ht·hr/d between the direct and reflected waves becomes small, and the reflection coefficient at the ground is nearly −1, so the two waves almost cancel. Working out the small difference that remains gives Pr ≈ PtGtGr(ht·hr)²/d⁴, inversely proportional to the fourth power of distance and containing no wavelength (frequency). Doubling the distance cuts it to 1/16, a fall of about 12 dB. The free-space square law holds only closer than the breakpoint (about 4ht·hr/λ), where interference between the two waves makes the received power rise and fall in peaks and nulls. The cancellation grows with distance, so the power is not constant either. The model also shows that raising the antennas increases the received power at long range. Note, however, that the breakpoint moves farther out at higher frequencies, so the distance at which the fourth-power law begins depends on frequency.

fading-014.question: Indoor and outdoor path loss is expressed as PL(d) = PL(d0) + 10n log₁₀(d/d0) dB. With a loss of 40 dB at the reference distance d0 = 1 m and a path loss exponent n = 3, what is the path loss at a distance of 100 m?
choices: 80 dB
160 dB
100 dB
fading-014.explanation: PL = 40 + 10 × 3 × log₁₀(100/1) = 40 + 30 × 2 = 100 dB. The loss rises by 10n = 30 dB for every tenfold increase in distance. 80 dB is the value calculated for free space with n = 2; in urban areas without line of sight and indoors, obstruction and scattering make n larger than 2, and values of about 3 to 4 are commonly used. 160 dB wrongly uses 20n instead of 10n; it is a power ratio, so the factor is 10 (the 20 log in the free-space formula is the form that already includes n = 2). The path loss exponent is an empirical value that varies with the environment, so it is chosen to fit measurements.

fading-015.question: Suppose the variation of the local mean received level due to shadowing follows a normal distribution in dB (a log-normal distribution) with a standard deviation of 8 dB. At the cell edge, which is closest to the margin to add to the average path loss so that the local mean received level exceeds the required value at 90% of locations? Take the upper 10% point of the standard normal distribution as 1.28.
choices: About 10 dB
8 dB
About 16 dB
fading-015.explanation: The probability that the received level (in dB) falls 1.28σ or more below the mean is 10%, so a margin of 1.28 × 8 ≈ 10.2 dB keeps it above the required value at 90% of locations. With 8 dB (1σ), the probability of falling below is about 16%, so it exceeds the requirement at only about 84% of locations. About 16 dB (2σ) corresponds to about 97.7% of locations, more than the 90% condition needs. The standard deviation of shadowing varies with the environment, and values of about 6 to 10 dB are commonly used in urban areas. This margin is considered separately from the margin for the fast fluctuation of Rayleigh fading.
